index.title: Omniweave — a local 6-in-1 editor that doesn't break your originals
index.description: A free, open-source (GPL-3.0) editor with a ~17 MB installer that never uploads your files. Open, edit and save raster, vector (AI), PDF, DOCX, HWPX, slides and PSD on one canvas.
index.ogTitle: Omniweave — a local 6-in-1 editor that doesn't break your originals

proof.h2:
Only what we measured.
And what doesn't work yet.
proof.lead: Every number below comes from an actual run, with its conditions. Work that is still in progress is marked “in progress”.

size.d: Windows x64 installer, 0.1.0 development build (10,239,987 bytes). Rendering uses WebView2, which ships with Windows.

corpus.d: 65 succeeded · 8 partial · 0 failed · 8 unsupported with an explanation. “Partial” means cases like legacy DOC/HWP (text and tables only) or PSD (effects and adjustments excluded).

local.k: Servers your files are sent to
local.d: Opening, editing, saving, converting and the quick tools all run on your PC. The network is used only to check for new versions (GitHub Releases).

crypto.d: PDF (AES-256) · DOCX/XLSX/PPTX (Office Agile) · .omw (AES-256-GCM). Edited files are re-encrypted on save; re-encrypted Office files were verified to open in Microsoft Office 16.

proof.formats: Documents, spreadsheets, slides, images, PSD, video, audio, e-books, text and code. Each format states its support level (full, partial, or an explanation).
proof.history: Every command since you started is recorded. Preview any point and jump back in one step; the history is saved inside the .omw.
proof.tools: Merge PDFs, shrink PDFs, PDF→JPG, images→PDF, shrink photos, batch JPG conversion — processed on your PC instead of an upload website.
proof.losslessH: Lossless save of originals in progress
proof.lossless: Goal: parts you didn't edit are saved byte-for-byte as in the original. In progress for PDF and PSD; DOCX and HWPX are on the roadmap. Today, saving DOCX/HWPX writes a new document from what Omniweave understood.
proof.sign: Current builds are not code-signed yet, so SmartScreen may warn on first run. The download page explains how to verify files with SHA-256.
proof.ui: The app UI is available in Korean, English, Japanese and Chinese: pick one in the installer and change it any time in Preferences. This website is available in the same four languages.
proof.note: Sample results copy only the counts from test-corpus/REPORT.md (file contents and names are not published). Installer size is from a development build and may change per release.

why.lead: An image editor, an illustration tool, a PDF editor, two word processors (DOCX and HWPX), a slide app. You paste the same logo six times and re-fit the same paragraph six different ways.
why.s3: Tweak the position, size, color, opacity and font of whatever is selected
why.claim: Different names, same work. Pages or layers, vectors or bitmaps — in the end that only decides how the result is saved. It doesn't matter while you're editing.

matrix.caption: What your hands actually do is the same in all six. What differs is feature depth and the file format.

mods.h2:
Six kinds of work,
one scene graph.
mods.lead: Raster tiles, Bézier paths, text paragraphs, tables, PDF pages, images and video are all the same kind of node. Only what is implemented in code today is listed. Depth per format is where we compete.

loom.lead: Every pixel tile, node and asset has its own 64-bit content address. The screen, saving and undo are all functions of those addresses.
loom.thread: Content addresses for 256 px pixel tiles, nodes and assets. Identical tiles are stored once, and on open every hash is recomputed so only damaged pieces get skipped.
loom.weave: A screen tile's key is the hash of the pieces that touch it. With no dirty flags and no invalidation code, “I erased it but it's still on screen” bugs simply can't happen by design.
loom.shuttle: Writes only never-seen pieces to IndexedDB, incrementally. Autosave stays light, and you can recover after a crash.
loom.history: Undo just swaps an immutable document reference. No pixels are copied, so its cost doesn't grow with document size.
loom.canvasAria: Illustration: a grid of 40 screen tiles on the left; on the right the tiles unravel into three threads — violet, teal and coral. Rubbing the grid redraws only the tiles you touch.
loom.statInit: Rub the grid. Only the screen tiles you touch get redrawn.

metrics.m2d: Raw RGBA 51.3 MiB → 10.5 MiB deduped → saved
metrics.m4d: A deep copy of the same 4K document (structuredClone) takes 24–28 ms
metrics.note: Measured with bench/loom.bench.ts (Vitest bench, Node, DOM-free code paths) on synthetic documents; real documents may differ. Machine: Intel Core Ultra 5 125H, Windows 11, Node v24.13.1 · range of means over two runs (other work was running, so variance is high) · save→open round trip: 0 corrupt · 0 missing · document root address matches. Rendering (canvas drawing) time is not included — the Loom meter in the app's status bar shows it live. Reproduce with npm run bench.

omw.lead: .omw (Omniweave Workspace Package) is a plain zip container. Identical tiles go in once, along with copies other tools can read.
omw.t2: metadata, Loom root address, page index
omw.t3: unified scene graph (pixels as tile addresses)
omw.t10: plain text for search and indexing
omw.f1: Every tile and asset hash is recomputed. Pieces that don't match are skipped and counted, and the rest of the document opens normally.
omw.f2h: Only two things are needed to open it
omw.f2: Omniweave reads just scene_graph.cbor and the content-addressed pieces. Everything else is a read-only copy for other tools.
omw.f3: The installer associates .omw with Omniweave, so a double-click opens it.

faq.lead: We're in early development, so here is what works and what doesn't — up front.

items.q: Does it fully replace the existing programs?
items.a: No. The goal is an integrated editor for many formats in one place, and depth per format is where we compete. Specialist features such as advanced filters, print separations, equation editors and track changes are out of scope today.

items.q: What exactly does “doesn't break your originals” mean?
items.a:
The direction is: parts you didn't edit are saved exactly as in the original. Honestly, today:

  • In progress: original-preserving save for PDF and PSD.
  • Roadmap: original-preserving (pass-through) save for DOCX and HWPX.
  • Today: saving to DOCX/HWPX writes a new document from what Omniweave understood (paragraphs, character formatting, table objects). Elements such as footnotes and headers can be lost.
  • Encrypted documents are re-encrypted when saved.

items.q: Will DOCX/HWPX files look exactly like the original?
items.a:
Import is paragraph- and character-format centric (alignment, line spacing, font, size, color, bold/italic/underline). Not yet supported or simplified:

  • Tables inside DOCX/HWPX are not yet imported as tables; they flatten into paragraphs.
  • Footnotes/endnotes, headers/footers, page numbers, style inheritance, TOC, tracked changes.
  • Embedded pictures, shapes and equations.
  • Pagination is recomputed with A4 layout and may differ from the original.

Pages render as-is; “text elevation” turns the text into line-level text objects you can edit, covering the original glyphs with a background-colored rectangle. Text over complex backgrounds and reflowing columns or tables are not supported yet.

PDF export in the current release embeds each page as an image. Export with live text is in progress.

items.q: How far do PPTX, legacy HWP and PSD go?
items.a:
• PPTX: opens text, shapes, pictures, tables and backgrounds as slides and saves back to PPTX. Some picture formats such as EMF are skipped and some shapes are approximated as rectangles.
  • Legacy HWP/DOC/PPT: body text and table contents only. For formatting and pictures, save as HWPX/DOCX/PPTX in the original program first.
  • PSD: opens pixel layers and the composite image. Layer effects, adjustment layers and the text engine are excluded.

items.q: Are my files really never uploaded?
items.a: Yes. Opening, editing, saving, converting and the quick tools all run on your PC, and the autosave journal is local. The network is used only to check for new versions (GitHub Releases), and this website has no tracking or analytics scripts. The source is open, so you can verify it.

items.q: Can I try it without installing?
items.a: The same app runs in a web browser. When the browser demo goes public, a “Try it now — no install” button appears on this page. The demo also processes files inside your browser, without sending them to a server.

Not yet — it is Canvas 2D + TypeScript. A WebGPU renderer and a Rust/WASM core are on the roadmap. Today's speed comes from Loom's “repaint and re-save only what changed” structure. The Loom table is everything we claim.

items.q: Is there an English UI? What about macOS and Linux?
items.a: Yes. The app UI comes in Korean, English, Japanese and Simplified Chinese: pick one in the installer and change it any time in Preferences. macOS and Linux builds are marked experimental until verified on real machines. Officially supported: Windows 10·11 and running in the browser.

One thread at a time —
weave it with us.
oss.lead: Issues and pull requests are welcome. The most helpful thing of all: real files that break.

oss.w2: TypeScript (strict) · React · Tauri 2. Dev setup and commit rules are in CONTRIBUTING.md.
oss.w3: No reverse engineering of third-party binaries — only public standards (ISO 32000, ECMA-376, KS X 6101).

name.p1: “Ome!” (Oh-meh) is what people in Jeolla, in southwestern Korea, blurt out when something surprises or amazes them — the local way of saying “Oh my!” or “Wow!”. Even many Koreans from other regions know it only from friends or TV.
name.p2: It's also the first letters of Omniweave (OM-niweave → Ome). The name holds that little gasp you let out the first time you see images, documents, PDFs and slides all working on one canvas.
name.quote: “All of it, in one file? Ome!”

ss.h: If you see “Windows protected your PC”
ss.browser: When downloading: if Edge or Chrome says the file “isn’t commonly downloaded”, open the download list, choose … next to the file and pick Keep (Chrome: Keep or Download anyway). The warning appears because the app is new and has few downloads yet.
ss.unsigned: Current builds are not code-signed yet, so Microsoft Defender SmartScreen may block the first launch. If you downloaded the file from this page (GitHub Releases) and the checksum below matches:
ss.signed: The installer is code-signed. If SmartScreen still shows a warning, you can run it like this:
steps: Check that the app name is Omniweave.
ss.warn: If you got the file from anywhere else, don't run it.

up.manual: Automatic updates are coming. They're planned for the installer; until then:
steps: Download the new installer from this page.
Run it to install over the old version. Your work files (.omw) are left untouched.
up.portable: For the portable build, just replace the exe with the new one.
up.auto: The installer and the portable build check for new versions on their own. When one is available, the app downloads and verifies it, lets you know, and updates once you confirm. The Microsoft Store version is updated by the Store.
up.autoPortable: The portable build replaces its own exe in place (same name and folder) after checking its size, SHA-256 and signature. If its folder is read-only, it opens this page instead.

ck.p2: , which lists the SHA-256 hash of each file. If the value you compute matches it character for character, the file wasn't altered on the way to you.
ck.winNote: Compare the Hash with the same file's line in SHA256SUMS.txt (case doesn't matter)
ck.unix: On macOS and Linux, put SHA256SUMS.txt next to the downloaded file and run the command — matching files are reported as OK.

req.wv: Built into Windows 11. If it's missing on Windows 10, the installer downloads and installs it during setup (internet connection required). The portable build only runs where WebView2 is already installed.
req.perm: Installs for the current user, so no administrator rights are needed.
req.web: Node.js 18+ and a recent Chromium-based browser, Firefox or Safari
req.other: Experimental builds — we'll list supported versions here once they've been verified on real machines.
req.note: This is an early preview. Keep a separate copy of any important document you open with it. Import limits are covered in the honest FAQ.
